questions.question: How is $x^{1/n}$ defined?
options: As the infimum of all real y such that y^n ≥ x
As any real number y satisfying y^n = x
As the supremum of all real y such that y ≥ 0 and y^n ≤ x
As the average of x and n

questions.question: Using the course convention for odd roots, what is $(-8)^{1/3}$?
options: It is not real.

questions.question: What is $\sqrt{4}$?
For $x=\tfrac14$ and $n=2$, which statement is correct?
options: $x^{1/2}$ is undefined

questions.question: Defining $x^{1/n}$ as a supremum relies on which property of the real numbers?
options: It first assumes the usual exponent laws for rational exponents
It chooses any solution of $y^n=x$ without fixing the sign
It defines roots using order properties of the real numbers
It works only when $x$ is already known to be a perfect $n$-th power

questions.question: Which monotonicity property does the $n$-th root function have on $[0,+\infty)$?
options: It is decreasing on $[0,+\infty)$.
It is increasing only when $n$ is even.
It is defined only for perfect $n$-th powers.
It is increasing on $[0,+\infty)$.

questions.question: Suppose 0 ≤ a ≤ b and n ≥ 1 is a positive integer. What follows from the increasing property of the n-th root function?
options: a^($\frac{1}{n}$) = b^($\frac{1}{n}$) always
a^($\frac{1}{n}$) is undefined

questions.question: Using the definition, what is 0^($\frac{1}{n}$) for n ≥ 1?
options: n
It is not defined because 0 is not positive

questions.question: Why is the condition y ≥ 0 included in the defining set for x^($\frac{1}{n}$)?
options: To select the nonnegative root rather than a negative one
To force the defining set to be empty for every $x$
To guarantee that the index $n$ comes out negative
To restrict the argument $x$ to a positive integer

questions.question: Which statement gives the real-domain rule for $n$-th roots when $n$ is a positive integer?
options: Every positive integer index allows every real input $x$.
Every positive integer index requires a nonnegative input $x$.
Even indices allow all real inputs; odd indices require $x\ge0$.
Even indices require $x\ge0$; odd indices allow every real $x$.

questions.question: Using the definition, what is x^(1/1) for x ≥ 0?
options: x

questions.question: For x = 4 and n = 2, which number belongs to the defining set {y in R: y ≥ 0 and y^2 ≤ 4}?
For $x\ge0$, what is $\left(x^{1/n}\right)^n$?
options: $x^n$

questions.question: What is $\sqrt{(-3)^2}$?
Why does the definition use $y^n\le x$ rather than $y^n=x$ in $\{y\ge0:\,\cdot\,\}$?
options: It yields a nonempty set bounded above, so the supremum exists
Because the equation $y^n=x$ can have several distinct solutions
Because using $\le$ makes the resulting root come out larger
Because the equality $y^n=x$ is in fact never attained

questions.question: The $n$-th root function is increasing on $[0,\infty)$. What does this guarantee?
options: Each $x\ge0$ has exactly one $n$-th root, so $x^{1/n}$ is single-valued
That $n$-th roots exist only for perfect $n$-th powers of integers
That $x^{1/n}$ may take several different values for one $x$
That the root decreases as the argument $x$ grows larger

questions.question: For $x=16$, compare $16^{1/2}$ and $16^{1/4}$.
options: both equal $8$

questions.question: Does the supremum in $x^{1/n}=\sup\{y\ge0:y^n\le x\}$ belong to the set?
options: Yes: $x^{1/n}$ satisfies $(x^{1/n})^n\le x$, so it lies in the set
No: a supremum is never an element of its set
Only when $x$ is a perfect $n$-th power
Only when $n=1$

questions.question: For $0<x<1$ and an integer $n\ge2$, how does $x^{1/n}$ compare with $x$?
options: It depends on whether $n$ is even

questions.question: Which fact guarantees that $\sup\{y\ge0:y^n\le x\}$ exists for every $x\ge0$?
options: The set is nonempty and bounded above, and $\mathbb{R}$ is complete
Every nonempty set of real numbers attains a maximum element
The set in question contains only finitely many points
The argument $x$ is required to be a rational number
